title: Whiter than snow: the luminous mind
hook: white shows every scuff. so is a stained mind stained for good?
carry: the mind is luminous; its stains are visitors
tomorrow: what does a patch of sun on a wall have to do with any of this?

segments.voice: Yesterday, red: the color before the story, and a fine peg to knock out an angry thought. Today, the last of the four colors, and a question bigger than paint.
screen: `RED: THE COLOR, THEN THE FINE PEG.` → `NOW: THE LAST COLOR.`

segments.voice: White sneakers show everything. One scuff on the first day and they never feel new again. A mind can seem like that too: one cruel thing said, one thing done that can't be undone, and it feels stained for good. That was yesterday's question: can a stained mind ever come clean? Today's disc is white: white flowers, white cloth, something of silver, the color that shows every mark. And a very old teaching answers more hopefully than the sneakers do.
screen: `ONE SCUFF, AND IT'S NEVER NEW.` → `STAINED FOR GOOD?` → `THE COLOR THAT SHOWS EVERY MARK.`

segments.voice: Here's the Buddhist answer, from a pair of very short suttas. The mind, the Buddha says, is luminous: bright, shining. It gets stained by defilements that come in from outside, like visitors: greed, anger, confusion. And it can be freed of them. The stain is real. It just isn't the mind's own color. A white cloth works that way too: dirt lands on it; it isn't made of dirt. Now a neighbor reaches for the same color. A psalm in the Bibles of both Jews and Christians says, in the King James words, "Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow." Two traditions, one image: a heart or a mind that can come clean, and a stain that doesn't have to stay. And one honest difference. In the psalm, the one praying asks God to do the washing; cleanness comes as mercy, received. In the suttas, no one is asked. The brightness is said to be there already, and the clearing is the work of practice, done by the one who practices. Each tradition says how in its own way, and neither needs the other to be wrong. What they share is worth saying out loud: a stain is not the whole story of a person.
screen: `THE MIND IS LUMINOUS.` · `STAINS ARRIVE LIKE VISITORS.` · `PSALM 51: WHITER THAN SNOW.` · `WASHED BY GOD, OR CLEARED BY PRACTICE.` · then, large: `WHITE.`

segments.voice: Take a plain white sheet of paper and rest your eyes on the white for a few breaths. Then, if you like, write one small word on it, a mark you'd like to set down. Look at how much white still surrounds it, and fold the page away.
White: odata in Pali. The color that shows every mark, and still isn't made of them.
Your line: the mind is luminous, and its stains are visitors. The stain is real, and it isn't the cloth's own color. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Theravada meditation the white kasina uses white flowers, cloth or a white or silver surface, noted as 'white, white'; the teaching that the mind is luminous and stained by visiting defilements is found in the Anguttara Nikaya.

options: Sort of: a sutta calls the mind bright, with visiting stains. But no one is asked to wash it.
Exactly the same thing. Every religion teaches this one idea, just in different words.
Not really. In Buddhism a stain is karma, so it stays with you for good, no washing.
chat.meaning: Both reach for white: a mind or heart that can come clean. The honest difference: the psalm asks God to wash; the sutta says the brightness is already there.

notes: Wisdom shape with the unity thread: shared image (white, a mind or heart that can come clean) in each tradition's own source (AN 1.49-52 paraphrased; Psalm 51:7 quoted from the KJV), plus one honest difference (the psalm asks God to wash; the sutta says the brightness is already there and practice clears the stains). No ranking; the script says neither needs the other to be wrong. A Keeper of each tradition should confirm the difference is described fairly.
Psalm 51:7 is numbered 51:9 in Jewish Bibles (JPS 1917); the script says 'a psalm in the Bibles of both Jews and Christians' and quotes the King James wording.
AN 1.49-52 numbering varies by edition (AN 1.51-52 in some). The 'like visitors' image renders agantuka (incoming, adventitious). Confirm.
Visuddhimagga 5 white kasina materials (white flowers, cloth, something of silver) paraphrased; confirm.
Practice is a hand-written word on white paper (varies the week's run of gazing practices); it is an invitation ('if you like').
